Persistence written to user shell init or systemd user units from AUR build/install scriptlet AIInstallation Medium
Hunts post-install persistence dropped by hijacked AUR packages — writes to ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, ~/.config/systemd/user/, ~/.config/autostart/, /etc/cron.d/, or /etc/profile.d/ when the writer's parent (or grandparent) is makepkg/pacman/yay/paru/trizen/pikaur/aura. Legitimate Arch packages rarely modify the invoking user's home directory. Rationale: Combines two article-grounded signals: the persistence file locations a build-time payload would naturally use (cron/systemd/shell-rc/profile.d/ld.so.preload) AND a writer that is an AUR helper or shell carrying a PKGBUILD/.install context. Legitimate AUR packages install to /usr/... — a write to ~/.bashrc or /etc/cron.d from makepkg's child is the differentiator.
ATT&CKT1546.004 T1053.003 T1547.013
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Shell-framework AUR packages (oh-my-zsh-git, bash-completion variants) that DO legitimately modify ~/.zshrc/~/.bashrc by design
  • AUR packages shipping legitimate systemd units to ~/.config/systemd/user/ (rare but exists — e.g. user-mode VPN clients)
  • pacman hooks updating /etc/ld.so.cache after a library install (different from ld.so.preload but path may confuse)
  • Dotfiles-management AUR packages (chezmoi, stow) intentionally placing files in home
  • First-time provisioning runs where a fresh user account gets its initial rc files populated by an install script
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "oh-my-zsh" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "bash-completion" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "chezmoi" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "stow"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the actual file content written — `cat` the persistence target and look for the malicious payload signatures (calls to /tmp/.* binaries, references to atomic-lockfile/temp.sh/fardewoak, base64-encoded blobs, ProcID hiding logic). Cross-check the source PKGBUILD against AUR upstream via `pacman -Qi` + `git log` on the AUR repo. 2) Contain: revert the persistence file to its pre-install state (or delete the rogue entry), kill any process started from it, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the AUR package name across the org to find every host that installed it; correlate with UC1/UC2/UC3 on the same DeviceId to confirm full kill-chain; remove and quarantine the package from local AUR caches.
let PersistencePaths = dynamic(["/.bashrc","/.bash_profile","/.zshrc","/.profile","/.bash_aliases","/.zprofile","/.config/systemd/user/","/.config/autostart/","/etc/cron.d/","/etc/cron.daily/","/etc/cron.hourly/","/var/spool/cron/","/etc/profile.d/","/etc/ld.so.preload","/etc/systemd/system/"]);
let AurTools = dynamic(["makepkg","pacman","yay","paru","trizen","pikaur","aura","fakeroot"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any (PersistencePaths) or FileName in~ (".bashrc",".zshrc",".profile","ld.so.preload")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (AurTools)
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (AurTools)
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("PKGBUILD",".install","post_install","pre_install","makepkg")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          Writer = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          WriterCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          WriterParent = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          PersistenceFile = strcat(FolderPath, "/", FileName),
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let PersistencePaths = dynamic(["/.bashrc","/.bash_profile","/.zshrc","/.profile","/.config/systemd/user/","/.config/autostart/","/etc/cron.d/","/etc/cron.daily/","/var/spool/cron/","/etc/profile.d/","/etc/ld.so.preload","/etc/systemd/system/"]);
let AurTools = dynamic(["makepkg","pacman","yay","paru","trizen","pikaur","aura","fakeroot"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (PersistencePaths) or TargetFileName in~ (".bashrc",".zshrc",".profile","ld.so.preload")
| where ActingProcessName has_any (AurTools)
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("PKGBUILD",".install","post_install","pre_install","makepkg")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          Writer = ActingProcessName,
          WriterCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine,
          PersistenceFile = TargetFilePath,
          TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AUR Install Scriptlet Writes Persistence to User Home or System-wide Auto-Start
id: e3f1b8a6-2c5d-4a9e-b7c4-6f8d3a2e1b9f
description: Detects file writes by makepkg/pacman/yay/paru/trizen/pikaur/aura (or a child shell carrying a PKGBUILD/.install context) that land in user-shell init, systemd user units, autostart, cron, profile.d, or ld.so.preload — the persistence locations expected from the Atomic Arch hijacked AUR packages.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

DeviceProcessEvents

| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.initial-access
logsource:

        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'

Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Hades on-import: Bun runtime download/execution chained from Python interpreter · [LLM] node-gyp spawning a shell, interpreter, or LOLBin during npm install · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Miasma and Hades Are Spreading Now: Detect Them on Developer Machines with Suspi
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Phantom Gyp: tiny binding.gyp written into installed npm package · [LLM] VS Code .vscode/tasks.json folderOpen auto-execute task dropped into project tree · [LLM] AI coding assistant config file dropped in project (.claude/setup.mjs, .cursor/rules/setup.mdc, .gemini/settings.json) · [LLM] PyPI package __init__.py modified with one-line obfuscated import-time hook (Hades pattern) · [LLM] File on disk matches known Miasma/Hades campaign SHA256 IOC · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phantom Gyp: tiny binding.gyp written into installed npm package AIInstallation Medium
Detects file writes of a binding.gyp into a node_modules subtree where the file is suspiciously small (Miasma's payload is ~157 bytes). The Phantom Gyp technique uses native-build hooks to execute code at npm install time, bypassing pre/post-install script controls. Rationale: Article explicitly names the technique ("Phantom Gyp") and the artifact size ("157-byte binding.gyp"). Native modules that legitimately need binding.gyp ship them at hundreds-of-bytes to multi-KB scale; a <500-byte one inside an installed package is the smoking gun.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer authoring a minimal new native binding (e.g. a Hello World native module) and committing a tiny binding.gyp into their own package
  • CI scaffolding tools (yo, generator-* templates) that emit boilerplate binding.gyp stubs into node_modules during prototype builds
  • Patched/forked native modules where a maintainer hand-trims the binding.gyp
  • Lerna/PNPM workspace hoist operations that copy stub binding.gyp from cache
  • Restored backups of dev workstations that replay file events at scale
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("yo.exe","node.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("generator-","--scaffold"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Read the binding.gyp content — Phantom Gyp embeds a JS command in a target/source/action field. Pull the parent npm install command line and the package name from FolderPath (segment after \node_modules\). Cross-check the package + version on the public npm registry vs. the workstation's package-lock.json. Step 2 (contain): Quarantine the workstation from the corporate registry, kill any running node/node-gyp processes, and revoke the developer's npm publishing token (npm token revoke) — Miasma steals tokens to self-propagate. Step 3 (hunt): Run UC6 (node-gyp shell-spawn) and UC7 (hash match) across the fleet for the last 14 days; pivot on the package name to find every other host that installed the same compromised version, and query DeviceNetworkEvents for any node.exe egress in the 5 minutes after the file write.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "binding.gyp"
| where FolderPath has "\\node_modules\\"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileSize between (20 .. 500)   // Miasma Phantom Gyp payload is ~157 bytes
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "binding.gyp"
| where TargetFilePath has "\\node_modules\\"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileSize between (20 .. 500)
| where ActorUsername !has "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256

VS Code .vscode/tasks.json folderOpen auto-execute task dropped into project tree AIInstallation High
Detects creation/modification of .vscode/tasks.json that the article identifies as an editor-side auto-execution vector for Miasma/Hades — VS Code runs tasks marked runOn:folderOpen the moment a developer opens the project. File-event-only detection because the payload is content-based. Rationale: Article's table explicitly lists .vscode/tasks.json (runOn:folderOpen auto-execute) and .vscode/setup.mjs (task-triggered setup script) as Miasma/Hades editor hijack files. The detection narrows to non-editor processes writing them (an npm install or tar extraction dropping a .vscode folder is the campaign's exact behaviour) — a developer hand-editing tasks.json comes from Code.exe and is filtered out.
ATT&CKT1546 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running `cookiecutter` / `degit` / `create-react-app` style scaffolders that drop a .vscode/tasks.json template
  • git checkout of a branch that adds .vscode/tasks.json (filter excludes git.exe, but powershell-driven git wrappers may still hit)
  • Repo-templating CLIs (`nx`, `nest new`, `vue create`) writing .vscode configs via node.exe
  • Restore from a workspace backup utility
  • Engineer using `npm pkg set` style tools to seed editor settings
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("cookiecutter","degit","create-react-app","nx generate","nest new"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the file content — Miasma's tasks.json uses runOn:folderOpen plus a shell command that fetches a remote payload. Identify the source archive: walk InitiatingProcessCommandLine for the .tgz / .whl / package.json being installed. Step 2 (contain): Block the developer from opening the project in VS Code (the trigger fires on folderOpen), revoke their npm + PyPI publishing tokens, and quarantine the affected workspace directory. Step 3 (hunt): Search the fleet for the same package name in package-lock.json / requirements.txt; for any host that opened the project after the file drop, hunt DeviceProcessEvents for Code.exe spawning powershell/cmd/curl/node in the 60 seconds after a Code.exe FolderOpen event.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FolderPath endswith "\\.vscode" and FileName in~ ("tasks.json","setup.mjs"))
     or (FolderPath has "\\.vscode\\" and FileName in~ ("tasks.json","setup.mjs"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","Code.exe","explorer.exe","git.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("npm","node.exe","yarn","pnpm","python","pip","tar.exe","7z.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has "\\.vscode\\"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("tasks.json","setup.mjs")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("code.exe","explorer.exe","git.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm","node","yarn","pnpm","python","pip","tar","7z","powershell","pwsh")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
title: VS Code tasks.json or setup.mjs Dropped By Non-Editor Process
id: 1b4d9f3e-6c2a-4f1b-9c08-7d3e9a0c6b12
description: Detects creation of .vscode/tasks.json or .vscode/setup.mjs by a package manager, archive extractor, or shell - matches Miasma/Hades's IDE auto-execute persistence vector.
references:

#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\\.vscode\\(tasks\.json|setup\.mjs)$/i NOT ContextImageFileName=/(\\Code\.exe|\\explorer\.exe|\\git\.exe)$/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

AI coding assistant config file dropped in project (.claude/setup.mjs, .cursor/rules/setup.mdc, .gemini/settings.json) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of AI-assistant auto-execute config files the article calls out by name. These run the moment a coding session starts (Claude Code SessionStart hook, Cursor rules load on open, Gemini settings injection) — a brand-new attack surface most EDRs do not yet baseline. Rationale: Article's verbatim table of IDE/AI-tool auto-execute files (.claude/setup.mjs SessionStart hook, .cursor/rules/setup.mdc, .gemini/settings.json, .vscode/setup.mjs, .github/setup.js) plus the explicit statement that these execute 'with the developer's own access and require no package install at all'. Filtering on non-IDE writers cleanly distinguishes attack drops from a developer hand-editing.
ATT&CKT1546 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dotfile-repo restore (chezmoi, yadm, stow) replaying these configs across new dev workstations
  • CLI installer for an internal AI-tool template ('claude init', 'cursor init')
  • Org-wide IDE settings deployment via SCCM / Intune script that drops .vscode/.cursor configs
  • Engineer cloning a project that legitimately ships .github/setup.js as part of its dev bootstrap
  • Container devcontainer.json onCreate that writes these files into a mounted workspace
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("chezmoi apply","yadm checkout","stow ","claude init","cursor init"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Read the file content — Claude Code's setup.mjs runs ES-module JS on every session start, so the body will contain a fetch/exec block if malicious. Identify the source package: walk InitiatingProcessCommandLine for the npm/pip/yarn install line and capture the package name and version. Step 2 (contain): Quarantine the workspace, force-quit any running claude/cursor/code processes for the affected user, revoke that developer's npm AND PyPI publishing tokens (the article notes Miasma/Hades steal both), and pin the malicious package version in the org registry blocklist. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the package name + version against package-lock.json / requirements.txt / pyproject.toml across the fleet (DeviceFileEvents for those filenames in the last 14 days); for any matched host, run UC4 (Bun-by-Python) and UC6 (node-gyp shell-spawn) and check DeviceNetworkEvents for the Bun runtime download URL.
let WatchedFiles = dynamic(["setup.mjs","settings.json","setup.mdc","setup.js"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName in~ (WatchedFiles)
| where FolderPath has_any ("\\.claude","\\.cursor\\rules","\\.gemini","\\.github")
| extend ConfigType = case(
    FolderPath has "\\.claude" and FileName =~ "setup.mjs", "ClaudeCode_SessionStart_Hook",
    FolderPath has "\\.claude" and FileName =~ "settings.json", "ClaudeCode_SettingsInjection",
    FolderPath has "\\.cursor\\rules" and FileName =~ "setup.mdc", "Cursor_RulesAutoLoad",
    FolderPath has "\\.gemini" and FileName =~ "settings.json", "Gemini_SettingsInjection",
    FolderPath has "\\.github" and FileName =~ "setup.js", "GitHubActions_WorkflowInjection",
    "unknown")
| where ConfigType != "unknown"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","code.exe","Code.exe","explorer.exe","notepad.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, ConfigType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let WatchedFiles = dynamic(["setup.mjs","settings.json","setup.mdc","setup.js"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName in~ (WatchedFiles)
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\.claude","\\.cursor\\rules","\\.gemini","\\.github")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","code.exe","explorer.exe","notepad.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256

Hades on-import: Bun runtime download/execution chained from Python interpreter AIExploitation Medium
Detects the Hades two-stage loader: a python.exe process (running an imported PyPI package's __init__.py) downloading a standalone Bun runtime and then executing it. Article explicitly describes this exact chain as the technique Hades uses to slip past EDR. Rationale: Article verbatim: 'the hook downloads a standalone Bun runtime and runs a JavaScript payload'. python.exe spawning bun.exe is a near-zero-false-positive process tree — Bun is a Node.js alternative that has no legitimate reason to be invoked from a Python interpreter. Adding the file-drop join cuts the few legit cases where a developer chains pip and bun for cross-stack tooling.
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1105 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Polyglot developer with a Python build orchestrator (e.g. invoke / pyinvoke / poetry script) that legitimately shells out to bun for a frontend build step
  • CI runner where a Python wrapper invokes bun as part of a containerised pipeline (more common on Linux)
  • Data-science workflow using a Python notebook to launch a JS-based visualisation server (rare but real)
  • Developer testing Bun runtime via a Python REPL one-off
  • Bun installer itself spawning bun.exe as a post-install smoke test under a Python-orchestrated installer
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("poetry run","invoke build","python -m build") and BunCmd has_any (" build"," run dev"," install"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Capture the Bun command line — the article says the JS payload reads secrets from process memory, so look for arg pointing to a fetched .js or eval/-e flags. Identify the Python parent's working directory (likely a developer project) and the imported package via the python -c or python -m args. Step 2 (contain): Kill bun.exe and the parent python.exe, isolate the workstation, and immediately rotate ALL credentials the developer has cached in env vars / .pypirc / .npmrc / git credential manager — Hades is memory-resident credential theft and has had whatever the Python process could read. Force-revoke npm + PyPI tokens. Step 3 (hunt): DeviceNetworkEvents from bun.exe in the same session for C2 destinations; DeviceFileEvents for the originating __init__.py (UC5); fleet-wide hunt for the same imported package in any host's site-packages directory.
let BunExec = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName =~ "bun.exe" or FileName =~ "bun"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe")
         or FolderPath has_any ("\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\","\\AppData\\Roaming\\","\\AppData\\Local\\Programs\\")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, BunPath=FolderPath, BunCmd=ProcessCommandLine, BunSHA256=SHA256,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath;
let BunDrop = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName =~ "bun.exe" or FileName =~ "bun"
    | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe","curl.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
    | project DropTime=Timestamp, DeviceName, DroppedPath=FolderPath, DropperImage=InitiatingProcessFileName, DropperCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
BunExec
| join kind=leftouter BunDrop on DeviceName
| where isnull(DropTime) or (Timestamp between (DropTime .. DropTime + 10m))
| project Timestamp, DropTime, DeviceName, AccountName, BunPath, BunCmd, BunSHA256, DropperImage, DropperCmd, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let BunExec = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where TargetProcessName =~ "bun.exe" or TargetProcessName =~ "bun"
    | where ActingProcessName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe")
         or TargetProcessName has_any ("\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\","\\AppData\\Roaming\\")
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, BunCmd=TargetProcessCommandLine, BunSHA256=SHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine;
let BunDrop = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where TargetFileName =~ "bun.exe" or TargetFileName =~ "bun"
    | where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
    | where ActingProcessName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe","curl.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
    | project DropTime=TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DropperImage=ActingProcessName, DropperCmd=ActingProcessCommandLine;
BunExec
| join kind=leftouter BunDrop on DvcHostname
| where isnull(DropTime) or (TimeGenerated between (DropTime .. DropTime + 10m))
| project TimeGenerated, DropTime, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, BunCmd, BunSHA256, DropperImage, DropperCmd, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

PyPI package __init__.py modified with one-line obfuscated import-time hook (Hades pattern) AIInstallation Medium
Detects writes to a __init__.py inside a site-packages tree where the file contains a single long obfuscated line with download/exec semantics — Hades's signature payload shape described in the article. Rationale: Article: 'The malicious code is an obfuscated one-line hook embedded in a package's __init__.py. The moment a developer imports the package, the hook downloads a standalone Bun runtime'. The detection joins the file write (during pip install) with python.exe public network egress in the next 5 minutes (the on-import download). Sigma omitted: this is a cross-table correlation that the single-event Sigma model can't express.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine pip install of a small ML package that happens to import telemetry/auto-update logic from __init__.py (e.g. some PyTorch/HF wrappers do this)
  • pip install --upgrade on a package whose new version legitimately added an __init__.py rewrite + a network call (e.g. version check)
  • Editable installs (pip install -e .) where a developer iterates and the file changes repeatedly
  • Conda environment rebuild that rewrites all __init__.py files in a refreshed env
  • Air-gapped offline pip-wheelhouse rebuild that touches __init__.py file timestamps
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): cat the modified __init__.py from the host (read-only) — Hades's hook is a single obfuscated line, often base64 or zlib-wrapped, ending in exec/compile. Identify the affected package from FolderPath (segment under site-packages\). Correlate the network destination from the join — Bun runtime download URLs are the second-stage indicator. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host. Run `pip uninstall <package>` then purge ~/.cache/pip and any virtualenv site-packages copies. Rotate every PyPI + npm token the developer has cached, plus any cloud credentials in env (AWS_*, AZURE_*, GCP_*) — Hades is memory-resident credential theft. Step 3 (hunt): Fleet-wide search for the package name in requirements.txt / pyproject.toml / poetry.lock writes (DeviceFileEvents) in the last 30 days; for matched hosts, run UC4 (Bun-by-Python) and a DeviceNetworkEvents lookup for the C2 URL extracted in triage.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "__init__.py"
| where FolderPath has "\\site-packages\\"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe","uv.exe","poetry.exe","conda.exe")
// Hades's one-line obfuscated hook tends to land in a file that's notable for being short but not minimal
| where FileSize between (200 .. 8000)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
// Correlate with python.exe network egress within 60s (the on-import download)
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe")
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | project NetTime=Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, NetProc=InitiatingProcessFileName, NetCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine
) on DeviceName
| where NetTime between (Timestamp .. Timestamp + 5m)
| project Timestamp, NetTime, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, FileSize, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, NetProc, NetCmd, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let InitWrites = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where TargetFileName =~ "__init__.py"
    | where TargetFilePath has "\\site-packages\\"
    | where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
    | where ActingProcessName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe","uv.exe","poetry.exe")
    | where TargetFileSize between (200 .. 8000)
    | project WriteTime=TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessCommandLine;
let PyNet = ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where SrcUsername != "" and DvcHostname != ""
    | project NetTime=TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, Url;
InitWrites
| join kind=inner PyNet on DvcHostname
| where NetTime between (WriteTime .. WriteTime + 5m)
| project WriteTime, NetTime, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessCommandLine, Url, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| order by WriteTime desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\site-packages\\*\\__init__.py OR *\\site-packages\\*\\__INIT__.PY) AND @Image:(*\\pip.exe OR *\\pip3.exe OR *\\python.exe OR *\\python3.exe OR *\\pythonw.exe OR *\\uv.exe OR *\\poetry.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\site-packages\\.*\\__init__\.py$/i ContextImageFileName=/(pip|pip3|python|python3|pythonw|py|uv|poetry)\.exe$/i WrittenBytes>200 WrittenBytes<8000 | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, WrittenBytes, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path values(Filesystem.file_size) as file_size values(Filesystem.process_name) as parent_process from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="__init__.py" Filesystem.file_path="*\\site-packages\\*" Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified") Filesystem.process_name IN ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","uv.exe","poetry.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_size | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where file_size>200 AND file_size<8000 | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path values(Filesystem.file_size) as file_size values(Filesystem.process_name) as parent_process from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="__init__.py" Filesystem.file_path="*\\site-packages\\*" Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified") Filesystem.process_name IN ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","uv.exe","poetry.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_size | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where file_size>200 AND file_size<8000 | sort - lastTime
node-gyp spawning a shell, interpreter, or LOLBin during npm install AIExploitation Medium
Detects the actual code-execution consequence of Phantom Gyp: node-gyp (the Node native-build helper) spawning processes outside its legitimate child set (python.exe, msbuild.exe, cl.exe, link.exe). Anything beyond those is Miasma's binding.gyp triggering arbitrary commands. Rationale: Article explicitly: 'a 157-byte binding.gyp file that triggers code execution during npm install through the native build step'. node-gyp's legitimate child set on Windows is python.exe + cl.exe + link.exe + msbuild.exe + node.exe (for sub-builds); spawning a shell or network LOLBin is the smoking gun of arbitrary execution. Pairing the parent (node + node-gyp/binding.gyp in cmdline) with the suspicious child set keeps this surgical.
ATT&CKT1059 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate native module whose binding.gyp action runs a small shell script for pre-build asset generation (e.g. some FFI bindings)
  • node-gyp invoking bash.exe on WSL-integrated Windows for cross-platform builds
  • Internal tooling that wraps node-gyp with a powershell wrapper for environment setup
  • CI provisioning script that explicitly shells out via curl from a binding.gyp action (rare)
  • Developer debugging a native module build by injecting `print`/`echo` commands
Suppression filter
| where not (ParentCmd has_any ("--verbose","--debug") and ChildCmd has "echo ")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the child command line and the parent's binding.gyp path from the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — extract the package name from the path segment under \node_modules\. Read the binding.gyp content (UC1 hit may already exist for the same path). Step 2 (contain): Kill the entire process tree, isolate the host, revoke the developer's npm token, pin the malicious package version in the registry blocklist. Step 3 (hunt): Fleet-wide hunt for the same package version in package-lock.json writes (UC3 cross-pivot); pivot the resolved C2 host/IP from any child curl/wget/bitsadmin cmdline into DeviceNetworkEvents across all assets; check whether any token-bearing CI runners installed the same package.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
  and (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "node-gyp" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "\\binding.gyp")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage=FolderPath,
          ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName =~ "node.exe"
  and (ParentProcessCommandLine has "node-gyp" or ParentProcessCommandLine has "\\binding.gyp")
| where TargetProcessName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| where ActorUsername !has "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, SHA256

File on disk matches known Miasma/Hades campaign SHA256 IOC AIInstallation Medium
Straight IOC sweep against the five SHA256 hashes the article shipped for the Miasma + Hades campaigns. Includes the file-event match plus a process-execution match because the actor distributes via both file-drop and direct-execution paths. Rationale: Pre-extracted SHA256 IOCs from the StepSecurity Miasma/Hades coverage page. Hash-based detection is the highest-precision signal we can ship; unioning file/process/image-load tables ensures we catch the IOC whether it landed as a dropped artifact, executed payload, or loaded module.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst purposefully detonating a sample in a sandbox VM that ships telemetry to the same tenant
  • Security researcher with a malware corpus checked into a local Git repo (file event fires on clone)
  • Incident-response engineer copying a known IOC to a forensic share for analysis
  • Backup-system rehydration of a compromised host to a clean-room VM for triage
  • Defender for Endpoint sample-submission cache writing the same hash
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName matches regex @"(?i)(sandbox|malware|ir-vm|threat-research|honeypot)")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the host is a production developer machine, not an IR sandbox / researcher endpoint. Capture full process tree around the hash and the originating package source from InitiatingProcessCommandLine. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host immediately (alerting tier). Revoke that user's npm + PyPI + GitHub publishing tokens, plus any cached cloud credentials (AWS_*, AZURE_*, GCP_* env vars + ~/.aws/credentials + Git credential manager). The article says Miasma scans for publishing tokens specifically — assume any token accessible to the user process is exposed. Step 3 (hunt): Fleet-wide IOC sweep over the full 30-day retention window for the same hashes; pivot on the source package name (extracted from FolderPath under node_modules\ or site-packages\) to find every other host that installed the compromised version; check CI runners (GitHub Actions, Jenkins) for the same package since those carry org-wide publishing tokens.
let MiasmaHadesIOCs = dynamic([
    "dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe",
    "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d",
    "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c",
    "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655",
    "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966"
]);
union isfuzzy=true
    (DeviceFileEvents
     | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
     | where SHA256 in (MiasmaHadesIOCs)
     | project Timestamp, Source="DeviceFileEvents", DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FilePath=FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, ActorImage=InitiatingProcessFileName, ActorCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
    (DeviceProcessEvents
     | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
     | where SHA256 in (MiasmaHadesIOCs)
     | project Timestamp, Source="DeviceProcessEvents", DeviceName, AccountName, FilePath=FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, ActorImage=InitiatingProcessFileName, ActorCmd=ProcessCommandLine),
    (DeviceImageLoadEvents
     | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
     | where SHA256 in (MiasmaHadesIOCs)
     | project Timestamp, Source="DeviceImageLoadEvents", DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FilePath=FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, ActorImage=InitiatingProcessFileName, ActorCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
let MiasmaHadesIOCs = dynamic([
    "dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe",
    "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d",
    "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c",
    "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655",
    "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966"
]);
union isfuzzy=true
    (ImFileEvent
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
     | where TargetFileSHA256 in (MiasmaHadesIOCs)
     | project TimeGenerated, Source="ImFileEvent", DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine),
    (ImProcessCreate
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
     | where SHA256 in (MiasmaHadesIOCs)
     | project TimeGenerated, Source="ImProcessCreate", DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath=TargetProcessName, TargetFileName=TargetProcessName, TargetFileSHA256=SHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine=TargetProcessCommandLine)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966") or SHA1 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966") or MD5 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966") or SHA1 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966") or MD5 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Killing me gently: Inside Gentlemen’s EDR killer framework

ESET WeLiveSecurity
2026-06-18 8 use cases 1 technique 2 kill-chain phases detected

ESET Research shares the results of a months-long investigation into the suite of EDR killers maintained by the RaaS gang Gentlemen

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Gentlemen BYOVD driver file dropped to disk (eb.sys, nseckrnl.sys, ThrottleBlood.sys, havoc.sys, etc.) · [LLM] GentleKiller dropper executable in staging directory or AV-impersonating filename · [LLM] Kernel-mode service registration for Gentlemen BYOVD drivers (Havoc service / %TEMP%\*.sys ImagePath)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Mass termination of EDR/AV processes by single non-system process (GentleKiller behavioral) · [LLM] OxideHarvest credential stealer command-line pattern (-i hosts -u user -p pass -o output) · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Gentlemen BYOVD driver file dropped to disk (eb.sys, nseckrnl.sys, ThrottleBlood.sys, havoc.sys, etc.) AIInstallation High
Detects file writes of the specific .sys driver filenames associated with the GentleKiller / HexKiller / ThrottleBlood / HavocKiller variants documented by ESET. Each variant drops a named vulnerable or malicious driver before loading it, so the on-disk artifact is the earliest high-fidelity pivot. Rationale: Driver filenames eb.sys, nseckrnl.sys, ThrottleBlood.sys, havoc.sys, dmx.sys, etc. are explicitly named by ESET as artifacts of GentleKiller / HexKiller / ThrottleBlood / HavocKiller variants and corroborated by BleepingComputer + Huntress. Cross-checked against the SHA-1 list in the article. Excluded vgk.sys + GameDriverX64.sys to avoid Valorant/Vanguard FPs — those collide with legitimate gaming. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/ • https://www.huntress.com/blog/w2-malvertising-to-kernel-mode-edr-kill • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/18/eset-gentlemen-edr-killers/
ATT&CKT1068 T1014 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Safetica DLP installation creates stpm_old.sys / stpm_new.sys to its install path
  • Zemana Antimalware install drops dmx.sys
  • Qihoo 360 Total Security install drops 360netmon_wfp.sys
  • Forensic tool unzipping a sample collection containing one of these driver names
  • Security researcher loading a sample for analysis in a sandbox VM
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)\\Program Files(?: \(x86\))?\\(Safetica|Zemana|Qihoo 360|Baidu|Huawei|TechPowerUp|NSecsoft)\\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","installer.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("GentlemenCollection","\\Temp\\","\\AppData\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped .sys against the article's SHA-1 list; check ESET signature name on InitiatingProcessFileName. Pull DeviceProcessEvents for the dropper that created the file, look for matching Kasps.exe / FaceIT*.exe / EASolo*.exe / Deletor.exe naming. 2) Contain: isolate the host (MDE Isolate), kill the dropping process tree, block SHA256 of the .sys at the EDR layer, query all hosts for the same file. 3) Hunt: search the last 30d for the same driver across the org, pivot on the dropper's parent (often a ransomware loader or RDP session), look for ShadowCopy deletion and lsass dumps following the driver load — these precede encryption.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FileName in~ ("eb.sys","nseckrnl.sys","stpm_old.sys","stpm_new.sys","dmx.sys","360netmon_wfp.sys","G11.sys","googleApiUtil64.sys","ThrottleBlood.sys","havoc.sys","IMFForceDelete.sys")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
// Exclude legitimate vendor installer paths — Gentlemen drops to %TEMP%, %APPDATA%, %PUBLIC%, or staging dir
| where not(FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)\\Program Files(?: \(x86\))?\\(Safetica|Zemana|Qihoo 360|Baidu|Huawei|TechPowerUp|NSecsoft)\\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("eb.sys","nseckrnl.sys","stpm_old.sys","stpm_new.sys","dmx.sys","360netmon_wfp.sys","G11.sys","googleApiUtil64.sys","ThrottleBlood.sys","havoc.sys","IMFForceDelete.sys")
| where not(TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)\\Program Files(?: \(x86\))?\\(Safetica|Zemana|Qihoo 360|Baidu|Huawei|TechPowerUp|NSecsoft)\\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername,
          TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GentleKiller dropper executable in staging directory or AV-impersonating filename AIInstallation High
Detects execution of the standardized Gentlemen EDR-killer droppers — files named after the security product they impersonate (Kasps.exe, FaceIT*.exe, EAAntiCheat*.exe, BitD*.exe, Deletor.exe, HwAudKiller.exe, Symantec.exe, Sent.exe) and dropped from the 'GentlemenCollection' staging directory or user-writable paths. Combines naming convention with path constraint to suppress FPs from real AV binaries. Rationale: Dropper names (Kasps.exe, FaceIT*.exe, BitD*.exe, Deletor.exe, HwAudKiller.exe, Sent.exe, All.exe, buildx64.exe) and the 'GentlemenCollection' staging directory are explicit ESET findings. SHA-1 hash list (15 droppers) from the article is embedded for definitive hits. Path restriction to user-writable locations eliminates FPs from any legitimately-installed AV with similar names. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/ • https://socradar.io/blog/dark-web-profile-the-gentlemen-ransomware/

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware researcher detonating an ESET-supplied sample bundle in a sandbox VM
  • Red team operator using publicly-leaked GentleKiller samples for an authorized assessment
  • DFIR analyst zipping these artifacts into a triage bundle (extraction event)
  • Legitimate FACEIT anti-cheat installer running from %TEMP% during game install — distinct because real FaceIT.exe is signed and runs from \Program Files\FACEIT\
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has "SANDBOX" or DeviceName has "MALWARE-VM" or DeviceName startswith "DFIR-")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("7z.exe","7zg.exe","winrar.exe","explorer.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm SHA1/SHA256 against the article's hash list. Note which AV vendor the binary impersonates — this hints at what's running on the host. Check parent process: was it RDP-spawned, dropped by a script, or extracted from an archive? 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately (these tools precede encryption by minutes), kill the process tree, block the SHA256, and look at the host's Defender / EDR-vendor service state — Gentlemen typically kills the EDR right before launching ransomware. 3) Hunt: pivot on the user account and source IP — look for the same SHA1 across the org, RDP logons from the same source, recent share enumeration (SMB/445), Volume Shadow Copy deletion (vssadmin), and ransomware encryption indicators (mass FileRenamed events).

Kernel-mode service registration for Gentlemen BYOVD drivers (Havoc service / %TEMP%\*.sys ImagePath) AIInstallation High
Detects registry writes that create or modify a Windows service whose ImagePath references a Gentlemen-associated driver, OR whose service name equals 'Havoc' (HavocKiller's hardcoded kernel service name per Huntress + ESET). Drivers loaded via SCM service must touch HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services — this is the registration step, complementary to UC1's file drop. Rationale: Huntress writeup explicitly notes the HavocKiller driver is registered as a kernel service named 'Havoc'. ESET names the driver filenames that get loaded — registering a service with ImagePath pointing at one of those drivers is the ring0-load step. The service-name match alone is very low FP (no benign software uses 'Havoc'), and the ImagePath match catches the file-drop-to-load chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/w2-malvertising-to-kernel-mode-edr-kill • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/tax-search-ads-deliver-screenconnect.html
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1014 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate AV install (Safetica, Zemana, Qihoo 360) registering its own driver during MSI install — distinguishable by InitiatingProcessFileName=msiexec.exe + vendor-signed installer
  • Sysadmin manually copying a driver to %TEMP% for testing then using sc.exe create
  • Driver pack updater (Intel DSA, vendor utilities) registering an OEM driver under a non-standard service name
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","setup.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\Temp\\", "\\AppData\\", "\\Public\\", "\\ProgramData\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcess that wrote the ImagePath — if it's not msiexec/TrustedInstaller/sc.exe from a signed installer, treat as malicious. Read the ImagePath, then look for the corresponding .sys on disk and hash it. 2) Contain: stop the service (`sc stop <name>`), delete the registry key, isolate the host. Note: if the driver is already loaded, only a reboot fully unloads it — schedule one. 3) Hunt: across the org, find every host with the same service name or ImagePath; pivot on the dropping process's parent to find the C2/RMM that delivered it; check for the Gentlemen dropper hashes from UC2.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentControlSet\Services\"
| where (RegistryValueName =~ "ImagePath"
         and RegistryValueData matches regex @"(?i)\\(eb|nseckrnl|stpm_old|stpm_new|dmx|360netmon_wfp|G11|googleApiUtil64|ThrottleBlood|havoc|IMFForceDelete)\.sys")
   or RegistryKey matches regex @"(?i)\\Services\\Havoc($|\\)"
   or (RegistryValueName =~ "ImagePath"
       and RegistryValueData matches regex @"(?i)\\(Temp|AppData|ProgramData|Users\\Public|GentlemenCollection)\\[^\\]+\.sys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentControlSet\Services\"
| where (RegistryValue =~ "ImagePath"
         and RegistryValueData matches regex @"(?i)\\(eb|nseckrnl|stpm_old|stpm_new|dmx|360netmon_wfp|G11|googleApiUtil64|ThrottleBlood|havoc|IMFForceDelete)\.sys")
   or RegistryKey matches regex @"(?i)\\Services\\Havoc($|\\)"
   or (RegistryValue =~ "ImagePath"
       and RegistryValueData matches regex @"(?i)\\(Temp|AppData|ProgramData|Users\\Public|GentlemenCollection)\\[^\\]+\.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mass termination of EDR/AV processes by single non-system process (GentleKiller behavioral) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects a single user-space process killing 5+ distinct security-vendor processes from GentleKiller's 400-process target list within 5 minutes. The behavioral shape is the same regardless of which BYOVD variant is in play — kernel-driven termination of CrowdStrike, Defender, SentinelOne, Sophos, ESET, Kaspersky, Bitdefender, Trellix etc. is the unambiguous signal of an EDR-killer. Rationale: ESET documents 400+ processes across 48 security vendors targeted by GentleKiller — a single non-services.exe process terminating 5+ distinct EDR processes in 5 minutes has effectively no benign baseline. The behavioral threshold catches all GentleKiller variants regardless of which BYOVD is used, plus HexKiller/ThrottleBlood/HavocKiller, plus future variants. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/54-edr-killers-use-byovd-to-exploit-34.html • https://www.huntress.com/blog/how-attackers-disable-av-edr
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1489
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin running an AV uninstaller script (CrowdStrike CsUninstallTool, Sophos UninstallCLI) during product migration — typically initiated by msiexec/TrustedInstaller and signed
  • Endpoint Detection rollout where a Defender-replacement product disables Defender during install
  • EDR self-update sequence that briefly cycles its services
  • Sysadmin running pskill / taskkill against AV during troubleshooting (rare)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "uninstaller.exe" and InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "UninstallTool.exe" and InitiatingProcessFileName !has "CsUninstallTool" and InitiatingProcessFileName !has "UninstallCLI"
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess that did the killing; check its hash against the GentleKiller dropper list. If killer is unsigned, dropped to %TEMP%, or matches Gentlemen naming, treat as confirmed. 2) Contain: isolate the host (this is the last evasion step before encryption — minutes matter). Snapshot the disk if possible. Check VSS state — Gentlemen typically deletes shadow copies next. 3) Hunt: across the org, search for the same InitiatingProcess hash + the Gentlemen dropper hashes from UC2; check for the BYOVD driver drops from UC1; look for outbound C2 / file exfil from this host in the last 24h; correlate with any recent VPN / RDP logon from the same source IP.
let EDRTargets = dynamic([
  "msmpeng.exe","mssense.exe","securityhealthservice.exe","smartscreen.exe",
  "csfalconservice.exe","csfalcondaterepair.exe","csfalconcontainer.exe",
  "sentinelagentworker.exe","sentinelstaticengine.exe","sentinelagent.exe","sentinelhelperservice.exe",
  "sophosmtr.exe","sophoshealth.exe","sophosclean.exe","sophosfilescanner.exe",
  "avp.exe","klserver.exe","klnagent.exe",
  "bdagent.exe","bdservicehost.exe","vsserv.exe",
  "ekrn.exe","egui.exe","ecmd.exe",
  "mcshield.exe","masvc.exe","mfemms.exe",
  "avgsvc.exe","avgui.exe","avastsvc.exe","avastui.exe",
  "huntressagent.exe","huntressrio.exe",
  "carbonblack.exe","cb.exe","cybereason.exe","darktrace.exe",
  "traps.exe","cortex.exe","cyserver.exe",
  "tanium.exe","taniumclient.exe","threatlocker.exe",
  "deepinstinct.exe","diservice.exe","elastic-agent.exe","elastic-endpoint.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType == "ProcessTerminated" or ActionType == "ProcessKilled"
| where tolower(FileName) in (EDRTargets)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("services.exe","wininit.exe","system","taskhostw.exe","taskmgr.exe","msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\", "GentlemenCollection")
| summarize KillCount = dcount(FileName),
            VictimProcesses = make_set(FileName, 50),
            FirstKill = min(Timestamp),
            LastKill = max(Timestamp)
          by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
             bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where KillCount >= 5     // 5 distinct EDR/AV processes terminated in a 5-minute window
| order by FirstKill desc
let EDRTargets = dynamic([
  "msmpeng.exe","mssense.exe","securityhealthservice.exe",
  "csfalconservice.exe","csfalcondaterepair.exe",
  "sentinelagentworker.exe","sentinelstaticengine.exe","sentinelagent.exe",
  "sophosmtr.exe","sophoshealth.exe","sophosfilescanner.exe",
  "avp.exe","klserver.exe","bdagent.exe","bdservicehost.exe",
  "ekrn.exe","egui.exe","mcshield.exe","masvc.exe",
  "avgsvc.exe","avastsvc.exe","huntressagent.exe","cb.exe","cybereason.exe",
  "traps.exe","cortex.exe","tanium.exe","deepinstinct.exe","elastic-agent.exe"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventID == 4689   // process termination
| extend ExeName = tolower(tostring(split(ProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| where ExeName in (EDRTargets)
| where ParentProcessName !endswith "services.exe" and ParentProcessName !endswith "wininit.exe"
| summarize KillCount = dcount(ExeName),
            VictimProcesses = make_set(ExeName, 50),
            FirstKill = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastKill  = max(TimeGenerated)
          by Computer, ParentProcessName, Account, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where KillCount >= 5
| order by FirstKill desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:5 @Image:(*\\MsMpEng.exe OR *\\MsSense.exe OR *\\CSFalconService.exe OR *\\csfalconservice.exe OR *\\SentinelAgentWorker.exe OR *\\SentinelAgent.exe OR *\\SophosMTR.exe OR *\\SophosHealth.exe OR *\\avp.exe OR *\\klserver.exe OR *\\bdagent.exe OR *\\bdservicehost.exe OR *\\ekrn.exe OR *\\egui.exe OR *\\mcshield.exe OR *\\avgsvc.exe OR *\\avastsvc.exe OR *\\HuntressAgent.exe OR *\\cybereason.exe OR *\\traps.exe OR *\\cortex.exe OR *\\elastic-agent.exe) NOT @ParentImage:(*\\services.exe OR *\\wininit.exe OR *\\msiexec.exe OR *\\TrustedInstaller.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(MsMpEng|MsSense|SecurityHealthService|CSFalconService|csfalcondaterepair|SentinelAgentWorker|SentinelStaticEngine|SentinelAgent|SophosMTR|SophosHealth|SophosFileScanner|avp|klserver|bdagent|bdservicehost|ekrn|egui|mcshield|masvc|avgsvc|avastsvc|HuntressAgent|cb|cybereason|darktrace|traps|cortex|tanium|deepinstinct|elastic-agent)\.exe$/i
| _eventType="ProcessTerminated" OR ProcessEndTime!=""
| NOT ParentBaseFileName=/^(services|wininit|TrustedInstaller|msiexec)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, bin(_time, 300000)], function=[count(field=ImageFileName, distinct=true, as=DistinctKilled), collect(ImageFileName)])
| DistinctKilled >= 5
ENDPOINT
